title: Is MYP Extended Mathematics Graded the Same…
summary: Learn when MYP Extended Mathematics grades are globally standardized, where school practices differ, and how eAssessment boundaries work in practice.
body_markdown:
MYP Extended Mathematics is **not graded identically across every school in every context** . Authorized MYP schools use the same IB mathematics objectives and assessment criteria, but teachers create and mark most classroom assessments locally. Task difficulty, evidence collection, reporting methods, and teacher judgment can therefore vary.


Official **MYP Extended Mathematics eAssessment** is different. Candidates in the same examination session complete an IB assessment that is externally marked using a standardized process and session-specific grade boundaries. This article explains what is consistent, what can differ, and how to interpret each type of grade.


### The short answer: one framework, two grading contexts


MYP Extended Mathematics grading consistency depends on which result is being discussed.


Type of grade Who designs and marks it? Degree of standardization


Classroom assessment Designed and marked by the school Common IB criteria, but different tasks and judgments


School report grade Determined under the school's assessment policy Comparable in principle, but reporting methods may differ


Official eAssessment grade IB examination marked by IB-appointed examiners Internationally standardized for that subject and session


Two students can receive an internal grade of 6 after completing different work. By contrast, official eAssessment candidates receive grades through the same external process. An internal grade reports achievement within the school's programme, while an eAssessment grade is an **IB-validated result** .


### What remains consistent in MYP schools?


MYP Mathematics, including the extended pathway, uses four objectives and corresponding assessment criteria:


Criterion Mathematical performance assessed


**A: Knowing and understanding** Selecting and applying mathematical knowledge and procedures


**B: Investigating patterns** Identifying relationships, forming general rules, and justifying conclusions


**C: Communicating** Using correct notation, representations, terminology, and organization


**D: Applying mathematics in real-life contexts** Modelling situations, interpreting results, and evaluating solutions


Each criterion has a maximum achievement level of **8** and is equally weighted. Extended Mathematics uses the same broad criteria as standard Mathematics, but includes additional breadth, depth, and challenge. Students do not receive higher marks simply because they take the extended pathway; their work must demonstrate the relevant achievement descriptors.


The[official IB Mathematics subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/brochures-and-infographics/pdfs/myp-brief-mathematics-en.pdf) summarizes the objectives, criteria, content branches, and assessment structure. The IB's overview of[Mathematics in the MYP](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/curriculum/mathematics/) also explains how Extended Mathematics supplements the standard framework.


### Why internal grades can differ between schools


Internal tasks are created and marked by teachers. One school might assess algebra through a test and modelling investigation, while another uses an inquiry involving functions, graphs, and written justification.


Variation can result from:


- the content and complexity of the task
- the amount of scaffolding or calculator support
- the evidence used to determine final criterion levels
- the timing and frequency of assessment
- local conversions into percentages, letters, or national grades
- the school's published assessment policy


Teachers should apply the IB criterion descriptors through a **best-fit judgment** . This does not necessarily mean averaging every score from the term. A teacher may give greater significance to recent, comprehensive evidence when it better represents the student's current achievement.


Professional judgment remains involved, so schools should conduct internal standardization. Teachers might mark common responses, compare borderline work, and discuss how descriptors apply. This helps prevent one class from being judged more harshly than another.


### How an internal MYP grade is calculated


For school reporting, a teacher normally determines one final level for each criterion. The four levels are added to produce a **criterion total out of 32** .


Criterion Example final level


A 7


B 6


C 7


D 5


**Total** **25 out of 32**


A commonly used MYP conversion places a total of **25** in the **24--27** range, producing grade **6** .


Criterion total Common final grade conversion


0--5 1


6--9 2


10--14 3


15--18 4


19--23 5


24--27 6


28--32 7


Students should confirm that their school uses this table in its current assessment policy. Criterion levels are not percentages: level 6 does not simply mean 75%, and a total of 24 does not mean every task received 75%.


RevisionDojo provides further explanations in its[guide to MYP grade boundaries](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-myp-grade-boundaries-understanding-the-1-7-scale) and overview of[how MYP Mathematics is assessed](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-myp-mathematics-is-assessed-and-how-to-revise-for-it) .


### How Extended Mathematics eAssessment is graded


Students seeking an IB-validated Extended Mathematics result complete an end-of-course **on-screen examination** . Mathematics and Extended Mathematics examinations are externally marked rather than being teacher-marked assessments moderated afterward.


The examination includes three broad task types:


- **Knowing and understanding** , principally assessing Criteria A and C
- **Investigating patterns** , principally assessing Criteria B and C
- **Applying mathematics in real-life contexts** , principally assessing Criteria C and D


Criterion C appears throughout the examination. Accurate notation, connected reasoning, labelled representations, and appropriate mathematical language therefore matter across multiple tasks.


The official process is:


1. The candidate completes the Extended Mathematics on-screen examination.
2. IB-appointed examiners award raw marks using authorized marking instructions.
3. The marks are combined into a total raw score.
4. The IB establishes boundaries for Extended Mathematics in that examination session.
5. The raw total is converted into an official grade from **1 to 7** .


The IB confirms that on-screen examinations are[externally marked by trained examiners](https://ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/) . This creates stronger cross-school consistency because the candidate's own teacher does not determine the final result.


### Are eAssessment grade boundaries fixed?


No. Extended Mathematics boundaries can change between examination sessions. The IB considers candidate work, grade descriptors, examiner judgment, statistical evidence, and the demand of the assessment when awarding grades.


A more difficult examination may have lower raw-mark boundaries, while a more accessible examination may have higher ones. This is intended to preserve the meaning of each final grade, not to award grades to a fixed percentage of candidates. The IB's explanation of[student assessment and grade boundaries](https://ibo.org/university-admission/discover-why-ib-students-succeed/ib-student-assessment/) outlines this wider process.


Students must use boundaries for the **correct subject and examination session** . Boundaries from standard Mathematics, an older session, or a classroom conversion table cannot reliably predict an official Extended Mathematics result.


### What students and coordinators should check


Always identify whether a displayed result is an internal report grade, predicted eAssessment grade, or official IB result. These labels are not interchangeable. Schools should explain how criterion levels are determined, which conversion table is used, and whether students are registered for eAssessment.


For the full MYP Certificate, the IB currently requires eight assessment components, at least **28 points out of 56** , at least grade **3** in every required component, and completion of the school's service expectations. The[IB grading and awards page](https://ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/grading-and-awards/) gives the current certificate conditions. These requirements do not establish a universal pass mark for internal school reports.


### Preparing despite differences between schools


Prepare against the published mathematical skills rather than trying to reverse-engineer one teacher's percentages. After each task, identify whether marks were lost through mathematical knowledge, investigation, communication, or contextual application.


Effective practice should include procedural questions for Criterion A, justified general rules for Criterion B, complete notation and explanations for Criterion C, and modelling with interpretation and evaluation for Criterion D. eAssessment candidates should also practise completing extended problems in a timed on-screen format.


RevisionDojo's[MYP Extended Mathematics resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-extended-mathematics) and[Extended Mathematics Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-extended-mathematics/questionbank) support criteria-based practice. Students should still compare their work with teacher feedback, task-specific clarifications, and the school's assessment policy.


### Conclusion


MYP Extended Mathematics follows a shared IB framework, but internal grades are not perfectly interchangeable because schools design tasks and make reporting decisions locally. Official eAssessment results are more standardized because candidates take an IB examination, trained examiners mark it, and session-specific boundaries convert raw marks into grades from 1 to 7.


Students should distinguish criterion totals, report grades, predictions, and official results. RevisionDojo Study Notes and the Extended Mathematics Questionbank can then provide targeted practice for the content and reasoning assessed in both classroom tasks and eAssessment.
